entry.content:
Linux Device Drivers – Engineering Thesis

Practical introduction to Linux device driver development using SPI and I²C devices

This project was developed as part of my Engineering Thesis at AGH University of Krakow. Its main goal was to explore Linux kernel mechanisms used for hardware communication and to implement practical device drivers for external peripherals.

The project combines low-level programming in C with hands-on hardware development on a Raspberry Pi platform.

About the project

The work started with the fundamentals of Linux Kernel Modules (LKM) and gradually moved towards complete device drivers communicating with real hardware.

As part of the project, I implemented and explored:

  • Linux Kernel Modules and their lifecycle
  • Character device drivers and communication between userspace and kernel space
  • Device Tree and hardware description
  • Platform devices and platform drivers
  • SPI device drivers
  • I²C device drivers
  • REGMAP API
  • Hardware control directly from the Linux kernel

The individual stages of development were separated into dedicated Git branches, making it possible to follow the project from basic kernel modules to more advanced hardware drivers.

SPI

As part of the SPI section, I implemented drivers for external peripheral devices, including the MCP4921/MCP4922 digital-to-analog converter (DAC).

The project covers communication between the Linux kernel and SPI devices as well as the integration of hardware peripherals with the Linux device model.

I also explored communication with an I/O port expander using the Linux kernel REGMAP API.

I²C

The project also includes implementations of drivers for external integrated circuits communicating over the I²C bus.

This part allowed me to explore how the Linux kernel handles I²C devices and how hardware described through Device Tree can be matched with the appropriate kernel driver.

Platform Devices

In addition to SPI and I²C devices, I implemented practical examples based on Linux platform devices.

These included drivers used to control hardware such as:

  • LEDs
  • servo motors

This provided practical experience with the Linux device model and communication between kernel-space software and physical hardware.

Technologies

Programming: C
Operating System: Linux, Kernel 6.1
Platform: Raspberry Pi
Kernel: Linux Kernel Modules, Device Drivers
Hardware Description: Device Tree
Interfaces: SPI, I²C
Linux APIs: REGMAP, Platform Devices

What I learned

The project gave me practical experience with Linux development at kernel level and helped me understand how the operating system communicates with hardware.

It also allowed me to combine my electronics background with software development by working directly with physical peripherals connected through SPI and I²C.

The project became the foundation for my further development in Embedded Linux, Yocto and SoC-based systems.

Source code & Engineering Thesis

The complete source code, individual development stages and the full Engineering Thesis are available in the GitHub repository.

GitHub:
https://github.com/PawelZieba01/LINUX_Drivers_LKM_DT

entry.title: Smart Coffee Machine – ESP32 & Home Assistant
entry.summary: This project is a custom ESP32-based controller that integrates a Braun Tassimo coffee machine with Home Assistant. The goal was to add remote control and automation capabilities to a standard coffee machine using an external embedded system. The controller is based on an ESP32, and…
entry.content:
This project is a custom ESP32-based controller that integrates a Braun Tassimo coffee machine with Home Assistant.

The goal was to add remote control and automation capabilities to a standard coffee machine using an external embedded system.

The controller is based on an ESP32, and the application is written in MicroPython.

The Idea

The original coffee machine does not provide a network interface that could be directly integrated with a home automation system.

To determine the current state of the machine, the ESP32 monitors the LEDs located on its original control panel.

Based on these signals, the controller can determine what the coffee machine is currently doing and react accordingly.

This approach made it possible to add network connectivity and Home Assistant integration without replacing the original control electronics.

 

Coffee Machine State Detection

One of the key parts of the project is detecting the current state of the coffee machine.

Instead of using an internal communication protocol, the ESP32 monitors signals controlling the LEDs on the machine's original user interface.

These signals provide information about the current operating state and allow the external controller to react to changes during the brewing process.

Home Assistant Integration

The ESP32 communicates over the local network and integrates the coffee machine with a Home Assistant server.

The system provides several additional features:

• Remote coffee brewing activation over LAN
• Control through Home Assistant
• Scheduled coffee brewing
• Notification when the brewing process is complete
• Protection against starting another brewing cycle using the same capsule

This turns a conventional coffee machine into an IoT device that can be controlled and monitored as part of a home automation system.

Multithreaded Software

The MicroPython application uses two system threads operating simultaneously.

One thread is responsible for network communication, while the second handles interaction with the coffee machine and monitors its current state.

This separates network-related tasks from hardware interaction.

WebREPL

The project also supports WebREPL, allowing remote access to the ESP32 over the network.

This makes it possible to communicate with and program the controller without requiring a direct physical connection to the microcontroller.

Technologies

Microcontroller: ESP32
Programming language: MicroPython
Home automation: Home Assistant
Communication: LAN / WiFi
Remote access: WebREPL
Architecture: Multithreaded application
Application: IoT / Home Automation

What I Learned

This project gave me practical experience in integrating an existing electronic device with an external embedded controller and a home automation system.

The main challenge was to understand the behavior of the original hardware and use the available signals to determine the current state of the coffee machine.

The project also provided practical experience with ESP32, MicroPython, network communication, multithreaded applications, hardware signal monitoring, remote device access, and Home Assistant integration.

Source Code

The complete source code is available on GitHub:

https://github.com/PawelZieba01/HA_LAN_Coffe_Machine

entry.title: FPGA Battleships
entry.summary: FPGA Battleships is a hardware implementation of the classic two-player Battleships game using two FPGA development boards. The project was developed as part of the Digital Electronics Systems 2 course during the 4th semester of Microelectronics in Technology and Medicine. The complete game logic, VGA…
entry.content:
FPGA Battleships is a hardware implementation of the classic two-player Battleships game using two FPGA development boards.

The project was developed as part of the Digital Electronics Systems 2 course during the 4th semester of Microelectronics in Technology and Medicine.

The complete game logic, VGA output, board state management, user interaction, and communication between players are implemented in FPGA logic.

The Idea

The idea behind FPGA Battleships was to create a hardware version of the classic game in which the complete history of shots is stored and displayed throughout the game.

The system consists of two Basys 3 FPGA boards, one for each player.

Each player places ten ships on their own board. After completing the placement phase, the players can start the game and take turns selecting fields on the opponent's grid.

After each shot, the FPGA boards store the result and update the corresponding fields displayed on the monitors.

The game continues until one player's ship counter reaches zero.

Game Logic

The main game logic is implemented using a Finite State Machine.

The FSM controls the different stages of the game, including ship placement, starting the game, player turns, shooting, board updates, and the end-game condition.

A separate player_ctrl module monitors user interaction, including mouse position and interaction with objects displayed on the screen.

The current state of both game boards is stored in dedicated memory blocks and accessed by the main state machine and the VGA pipeline.

FPGA-to-FPGA Communication

One of the most interesting parts of the project is direct communication between two Basys 3 FPGA boards.

Communication is based on two parallel 8-bit buses used to exchange grid addresses.

Additional control signals are used to indicate system readiness and shooting actions.

The architecture is symmetrical. Both FPGA boards run the same design and are connected using corresponding input and output signals.

Their behavior at any given moment depends on the current state of their internal game logic.

VGA Output

Each FPGA board generates a VGA signal for its own monitor.

The VGA pipeline reads the current state of the game boards from memory and displays the appropriate information on the screen.

Different colors represent the state of individual grid fields:

• Green – player's ship
• Blue – missed shot
• White – empty field
• Red – hit ship

Because the board state is stored in memory, the history of previous shots remains visible throughout the game.

Seven-Segment Display

The built-in seven-segment display on the Basys 3 board is used to display the ship counters.

During the ship placement phase, the player can see how many ships are still left to place.

During the game, the display provides information about the remaining ships.

Clock Architecture

The project uses two clock frequencies generated by the clk_wiz_0 module.

The 65 MHz clock is used for the VGA pipeline and seven-segment display.

The 10 MHz clock is used for the main state machine, control logic, and communication with the second Basys 3 board.

This separates the video-related logic from the main game and communication logic.

Technologies

FPGA platform: Digilent Basys 3
HDL: Verilog
FPGA development: Xilinx Vivado
Digital design: RTL, Finite State Machines
Video output: VGA
Communication: Parallel FPGA-to-FPGA interface
User interface: Mouse, VGA display, seven-segment display
Clock frequencies: 65 MHz / 10 MHz

What I Learned

This project gave me practical experience in designing a larger digital system implemented entirely in FPGA logic.

It allowed me to work with RTL design, Finite State Machines, VGA signal generation, memory-based state management, user interaction, multiple clock frequencies, and direct communication between two FPGA boards.

An especially interesting part of the project was designing a symmetrical system in which two FPGA boards run the same design while communicating directly and maintaining their own game state.

The project also provided experience in integrating multiple independent hardware modules into a complete working system.

Project Demo

A video demonstrating the working FPGA Battleships system is available here:

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rVNI9s45F6EAzhemcrMdzVRFoP97SPt7/view

Source Code

The complete RTL source code, simulations, FPGA files, and project documentation are available on GitHub:

https://github.com/PawelZieba01/FPGA_WARSHIPS

entry.title: Smart Beehive Scale
entry.summary: The Smart Beehive Scale is an IoT project designed to remotely monitor basic parameters of a beehive. The system is based on an ESP32/ESP8266 microcontroller and collects information about beehive weight, ambient temperature, and air humidity. The project was developed in MicroPython and combines several…
entry.content:
The Smart Beehive Scale is an IoT project designed to remotely monitor basic parameters of a beehive.

The system is based on an ESP32/ESP8266 microcontroller and collects information about beehive weight, ambient temperature, and air humidity.

The project was developed in MicroPython and combines several sensors, local data storage, and GSM communication in a single embedded system.

Project status: Work in Progress

The Idea

Changes in beehive weight can provide valuable information about what is happening inside the hive. Combined with temperature and humidity measurements, this creates a simple monitoring system that can collect useful information without requiring constant physical access to the beehive.

The goal of the project was to create a standalone device capable of collecting these measurements directly at the hive, storing them locally, and providing remote communication.

Weight Measurement

The weight measurement system is based on a load cell connected to an HX711 module.

The HX711 provides an interface between the strain gauge load cell and the ESP32/ESP8266 microcontroller.

As part of the project, I developed a dedicated MicroPython module responsible for communication with the HX711 and acquisition of weight measurements.

Temperature and Humidity

Environmental conditions are monitored using a DHT11 sensor.

The sensor provides measurements of:

• ambient temperature
• relative air humidity

A dedicated MicroPython module was created to handle communication with the sensor and acquisition of environmental data.

Local Data Storage

The system includes an SD card reader for local measurement storage.

I developed a dedicated MicroPython module for SD card handling, allowing measurement data to be stored directly by the embedded device.

This provides local data storage independently of the external communication system.

GSM Communication

Remote communication is provided by a SIM800L GSM module.

A dedicated MicroPython module was developed to handle communication between the ESP32/ESP8266 and the GSM modem.

The use of GSM communication makes the concept suitable for locations where a traditional WiFi network may not be available.

Modular Software Architecture

The software was divided into separate modules responsible for individual hardware components.

Dedicated modules were created for:

• HX711 load cell interface
• DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor
• SD card storage
• SIM800L GSM communication

This approach separates hardware-specific functionality from the main application logic and makes individual parts of the system easier to develop and test.

Technologies

Platform: ESP32 / ESP8266
Programming language: MicroPython
Weight measurement: Load cell + HX711
Environmental sensor: DHT11
Local storage: SD card
Communication: SIM800L / GSM
Application: IoT, remote monitoring

What I Learned

The project allowed me to combine several different hardware interfaces into a single embedded system and develop dedicated MicroPython modules for external peripherals.

It also gave me practical experience with sensor data acquisition, load cell measurements, local data storage, GSM communication, and modular embedded software development.

The project is still under development, with the individual hardware modules forming the foundation for the complete beehive monitoring system.

Source Code

The source code and current development version of the project are available on GitHub.

GitHub:
https://github.com/PawelZieba01/Waga_ESP32

entry.title: BeeexAPI – IoT Data Collection & Visualization Platform
entry.summary: BeeexAPI is an IoT application designed to collect, store, process, and visualize measurement data from IoT devices. The project was created to explore the complete data flow between an IoT device and a server application, from sending measurements over the network, through storing them in…
entry.content:
BeeexAPI is an IoT application designed to collect, store, process, and visualize measurement data from IoT devices.

The project was created to explore the complete data flow between an IoT device and a server application, from sending measurements over the network, through storing them in a time-series database, to real-time communication with a web-based user interface.

The system consists of a Python/Flask backend, InfluxDB database, WebSocket communication layer, web interface, and a test client simulating an IoT device.

System Architecture

The application is divided into several independent components:

• IoT device / test client – generates measurement data and sends it to the server
• Flask server – provides HTTP endpoints and handles WebSocket connections
• InfluxDB – stores time-series measurement data
• WebSocket processing layer – handles requests from connected clients
• Web interface – allows users to visualize and analyze collected data

This architecture separates data acquisition, storage, processing, and visualization into dedicated parts of the application.

IoT Data Collection

Measurement data is sent to the server using an HTTP endpoint:

POST /<device>/save_data

The server validates incoming JSON messages and stores measurement points in the InfluxDB database.

A dedicated Python test client was created to simulate a real IoT device. It generates temperature and humidity measurements and sends them to the server, allowing the complete system to be tested without physical hardware.

Real-Time Communication with WebSocket

The web interface communicates with the backend using WebSocket connections.

Each connected client receives a unique identifier and two dedicated message queues:

• in – messages received from the client
• out – responses waiting to be sent back

Incoming requests are processed by a background processing_thread.

The communication layer supports several operations:

• get_data – retrieves measurement data
• get_mean – calculates average values
• get_max – retrieves maximum values
• get_min – retrieves minimum values

This approach separates WebSocket communication from database processing and allows multiple client connections to be handled independently.

Time-Series Data with InfluxDB

Measurement data is stored using InfluxDB, a database designed for time-series data.

The database layer provides functions for storing measurements, retrieving data for selected time ranges, calculating average values, and finding minimum and maximum values.

This makes it possible to efficiently store and analyze measurements collected from IoT devices over time.

Data Visualization

The project includes a web-based interface for interacting with the collected data.

The user can select an IoT device, define a time range, display temperature and humidity measurements, calculate average, minimum and maximum values, and visualize measurements on charts.

Communication between the interface and the server is handled in real time using WebSocket.

Message Processing

One of the more interesting parts of the project is the internal message processing mechanism.

Each WebSocket connection is assigned individual input and output queues. A dedicated background thread periodically processes incoming requests, performs the appropriate database operations, and places the results in the corresponding output queue.

This allowed me to experiment with multi-client communication, message queues, background processing, and separation of communication logic from data processing.

Technologies

Backend: Python, Flask
Communication: HTTP, WebSocket, JSON
Database: InfluxDB
Frontend: HTML, JavaScript
Architecture: Client–Server, message queues, background processing
Application: IoT data acquisition and visualization

What I Learned

BeeexAPI gave me practical experience in designing a complete communication path between IoT devices and a server application.

The project allowed me to work with HTTP-based communication between IoT devices and a backend, real-time WebSocket communication, time-series databases, message validation and error handling, background data processing, communication between multiple software components, and visualization of measurement data.

It was also an opportunity to look at an IoT system from a broader perspective, not only from the embedded device side, but also at the infrastructure required to receive, process, store, and present data generated by embedded devices.

Source Code

The complete source code, including the server, database integration, test client and web interface, is available on GitHub.

GitHub:
BeeexAPI – GitHub Repository

entry.content:
PV_DC_driver

Controller for a PV installation heating a hot water storage tank. Project in development and initial testing phase.

  1. Features
  2. Power Supply
  3. Enclosure
  4. MPPT Heater Control
  5. Voltage Measurement
  6. Current Measurement
  7. Temperature Measurement
  8. Control
  9. Pinout

Authors: Hardware - Paweł Z.    Software - Arkadiusz K.

Features

  • Heater control (on/off) --> MPPT PWM
  • 12V DC power supply - external adapter
  • Maximum PV panel voltage: 250V
  • Voltage measurement
    • on the PV panel
    • on the heater
  • Current measurement
    • on the heater
  • Power measurement
    • calculated from heater voltage and current
  • Temperature measurement
    • water in the hot water storage tank
    • in the controller enclosure / heatsink
  • Control
    • from the controller level -> display and buttons
    • over LAN - website or application
  • Data logging and visualization on the server
  • Hermetic enclosure

Power Supply

The controller will be powered from an external 12V DC voltage source with minimum 1A. Protection in the form of a medium-slow blow fuse 800mA 5x20mm.

  • Power Supply
  • Fuse

Enclosure

  • Hermetic box ZP180.120.90JPH TM ABS-PC KRADEX
    • Dimensions
  • Aluminum heatsink
    • Thermal resistance: 2 K/W
    • Dimensions: 150 x 50 x 25 mm
  • Round monostable button
    • 250V / 2A
    • LED backlight 2V
    • Mounting hole: 16mm
    • Mounting depth 20mm
    • Monostable
  • Microphone connector GX12 plug + socket
    • Mounting hole: 12mm
  • PG16 cable gland
    • Type: PG16
  • DC power socket 2.1/5.5mm
    • Inner pin diameter: 2.1mm
    • Outer pin diameter: 5.5mm
    • Mounting hole: 8mm
  • Backlit switch
    • 250V / 1.5A
    • LED backlight 2V
    • Mounting hole: 16mm
    • Mounting depth 25mm
    • Bistable
    • Documentation and dimensions
  • LCD display 16x2 with i2c converter
    • Controller: HD44780
    • i2c converter: PCF8574
    • Documentation and dimensions
  • 12V Buzzer
    • Power supply 9-15V
    • Diameter: 12mm
    • Height: 7.5mm

MPPT Heater Control

A PV panel behaves like a current source within a certain range. With excessive loading, voltage decreases and consequently power also decreases. With insufficient loading, voltage increases but current decreases, so power also decreases. Therefore, the load must be adjusted so that the maximum power of the panels is utilized at any given moment. We cannot regulate the heater resistance which is 'fixed', so we must regulate the current. Professional inverters use switching power supplies for this purpose, which allow voltage regulation on the load (thus also current regulation). Unfortunately, a power converter of about 2kW is too complex and the benefits of using it in our project are disproportionate to the time and effort. We will use PWM control.

Schematic diagram of heater control

  • PWM duty cycle: 70%
  • Panel current: 7A
  • Heater resistance: 17.63Ohm

The transistor switch will operate at 10kHz frequency, so by adjusting the duty cycle of the square wave we will be able to regulate the average current flowing[...] To prevent voltage changes on the PV panels from following PWM voltage changes, a capacitor bank must be used as an energy buffer. When the heater is off, energy from the panels will be stored in the capacitors (panels will charge the capacitors to their voltage). When the heater turns on, the capacitors will supply additional current and their voltage will not drop dramatically. In this way, we can regulate the average current of the load and the average voltage of the PV panels.

Through voltage and current measurements, we will learn the power at which the heater operates. To find the optimal operating point of the circuit, we will use an algorithm written in Python.

  • Transistor switch
    • Two parallel-connected N-mosfet transistors WMJ25N80M3
    • Galvanic isolation using optocoupler
    • Control voltage 12V
    • N-mosfet driver built from bipolar transistors

N-mosfet transistor driver

To ensure the fastest possible switching of the transistor switch, we will use a current buffer/amplifier, which will provide sufficiently high gate charging current. An additional stage with [...]

Voltage Measurement

ADC converter characteristic in ESP32

The ADC converter in ESP32 is not linear. Through experiments, it was found that 130mV should be added to the measurement result (operates in the range 130mV - 2500mV)
ADC converter calibration must be performed!!! Calibration instructions using the 'ESP32_ADC_calibration_tool'

Voltage measurement circuit on PV panels

  • Voltage measurement on the panel (buffer capacitor) using voltage divider (1:98.6)
    • Relatively precise voltage measurement in the range 13V - 250V (we assume maximum voltage 250V, while below 40V voltage we disable water heating)
    • Resistor values must be large so that large currents do not flow
    • R1=976kOhm, R2=10kOhm
    • For input voltage Uwe=250V, output voltage is Uwy=2.535V (according to simulation)
  • RAIL-TO-RAIL amplifier acting as voltage buffer
  • Low-pass RC filter with fg=33.86Hz (R=10kOhm, C=470nF)

Real-world tests

Tests will be performed on the finished prototype controller with attached panels.
At this point, it is known that the RC filter (R=10kOhm, C=470nF) behaves correctly at f=10kHz

Current Measurement

UNDER TESTING

Current measurement circuit - ACS712

  • For current measurement, we use the ACS712 sensor
    • Shop link
  • Low-pass RC filter with fg=33.86Hz (R=10kOhm, C=470nF)
  • *ACS712 can measure current flowing in both directions. For 0A current, it sets 2.5V on the output. Since ESP32 operates with 3.3V logic, we will connect the current converter 'in reverse' (0-20A -> [...]

UNDER TESTING

Current measurement circuit - 10mOhm shunt

  • To measure the current flowing through the heater, we will use a 10mOhm resistor as a series shunt.
  • Low-pass RC filter with fg=33.86Hz (R=10kOhm, C=470nF)
  • Using a non-inverting amplifier we will amplify the signal 10 times and shift (and invert) the signal by 0.5V up (2.5V - 0.5V --> 0A - 20A), so we will work in lin[...]
  • A protective stage (R14, D3, D4) was added against high voltage at the input of the first operational amplifier (in case the measurement resistor burns out, at the input of the op-amp there[...]

Real-world tests

  • Current measurement using the ACS712 circuit works much better at 3kHz PWM frequency (instead of 10kHz)

  • RC filter (R=10kOhm, C=470nF) and ADC calibration work at f=3kHz

  • ACS712 tested on a breadboard is very sensitive to external interference (including touching it)

  • Measurement accuracy obtained (voltage) approx. 100mV (approx. 1A)

  • Building a prototype measurement circuit on a 10mOhm shunt is in progress. We will check how the circuit behaves and with what accuracy it measures the flowing current.

Temperature Measurement

  • Water temperature in the boiler measured using DS18B20 sensor in a hermetic enclosure
    • To reduce the risk of incorrect reading (if the sensor is damaged), two such sensors will be used
    • Mounting using GX12 connectors
  • Temperature measurement inside the enclosure/heatsink also using DS18B20

Control

entry.summary: Android Remote RC Control via UDP A lightweight Android application that enables remote control of an RC vehicle using UDP communication protocol. The app provides an intuitive interface with dual analog joysticks and toggle buttons for basic vehicle movement and auxiliary controls. This is a…
entry.content:
Android Remote RC Control via UDP

A lightweight Android application that enables remote control of an RC vehicle using UDP communication protocol. The app provides an intuitive interface with dual analog joysticks and toggle buttons for basic vehicle movement and auxiliary controls.

Project Overview

This is a mobile control application built with B4A (Basic4Android) framework that communicates with an RC vehicle receiver (or any UDP-enabled device) via network sockets. The vehicle acts as a UDP server receiving control commands, while the app sends movement and state data in JSON format.

Key Features

  • Dual Joystick Control: Two independent analog joysticks for intuitive vehicle maneuvering

    • Left joystick: Vehicle power/thrust control
    • Right joystick: Steering/turning control

  • Auxiliary Buttons: Three toggle buttons for additional functions

    • Button 1, 2, 3: Custom vehicle functions (lights, special modes, etc.)

  • Battery Monitoring: Real-time battery level feedback from the remote vehicle

    • Receives battery status via UDP in JSON format
    • Displays current battery percentage

  • Network Configuration UI:

    • Manual IP address configuration
    • Custom remote port selection
    • Local listening port setup
    • Input validation (IPv4 format, port ranges 1-65535)

  • Landscape Mode: Full-screen optimized interface for comfortable landscape gameplay

How It Works

Communication Protocol

  1. Initialization Phase:

    • User enters remote device IP address and port in the main configuration screen
    • App validates IP format and port ranges
    • Proceeds to the control screen upon successful validation

  2. Control Transmission:

    • Joystick and button inputs are captured in real-time
    • Data is packaged into JSON format with the following structure: 
      {
  "Pos_X": -100 to 100,      // Steering input
  "Pos_Y": -100 to 100,      // Power/speed input
  "Btn1_state": true/false,  // Button 1 toggle state
  "Btn2_state": true/false,  // Button 2 toggle state
  "Btn3_state": true/false   // Button 3 toggle state
}
       
    • JSON payload is sent via UDP to the configured remote address and port

  3. Status Reception:

    • App listens for UDP packets on configured local port
    • Receives battery status from remote device in JSON format: 
      {
  "Battery_level": 0-100
}
       
    • Displays battery percentage in real-time on the control screen

Technical Details

  • Framework: B4A (Basic4Android) - Cross-platform rapid development framework
  • Protocol: UDP (connectionless, low-latency)
  • Data Format: JSON (human-readable, easily extensible)
  • Orientation: Landscape only (optimized for vehicle control)

Project Structure

B4A/               # Android application source (B4A project)
B4XMainPage.bas    # Configuration screen with IP/port setup
B4XPilotPage.bas   # Control screen with joysticks and buttons
Android_Remote_UDP.b4a  # Main project file
 

Usage

  1. Configure Connection:

    • Enter the IP address of your RC vehicle/receiver
    • Specify the remote port the vehicle is listening on (default: 1900)
    • Set a local port to receive battery feedback (can be 0 for auto-assignment)
    • Tap "Connect" to proceed

  2. Control Vehicle:

    • Use left joystick to control forward/backward movement
    • Use right joystick to control steering left/right
    • Toggle Btn1, Btn2, Btn3 for auxiliary functions
    • Watch battery level in real-time

  3. Return to Configuration:

    • Tap the back button to return to the connection screen
    • Modify settings and reconnect as needed

Input Validation

The app includes robust input validation:

  • IP Address: Standard IPv4 format validation using regex
  • Remote Port: Range 1-65535
  • Listen Port: Range 0-65535 (0 = auto-assign)

Dependencies

  • B4A core library
  • Network library (UDP support)
  • JSON library (data serialization)
  • B4XPages library (UI page management)
  • Joystick wrapper library (analog control)
  • Collections library (data structures)

Potential Applications

  • RC car remote control
  • Drone/quadcopter control
  • Remote robot operation
  • IoT device manipulation
  • Network-based device control experiments

Notes

  • Originally created as a hobby project to control RC vehicles from Android devices (January 2022)
  • Uses UDP for low-latency wireless communication
  • JSON protocol makes it easy to extend with additional sensors or controls
  • Can be adapted for any UDP-enabled remote device

Created: January 27, 2022
Last Updated: January 28, 2022

entry.content:
JABEL 031 Modified Power Supply

Overview

This repository contains comprehensive documentation and design files for a modified JABEL 031 power supply unit. This is an electronics project that includes PCB layouts, schematics, component lists, and AutoCAD drawings for the external enclosure design.

Created: June 25, 2021

 

Project Description

This project is dedicated to the design and modification of a JABEL 031 power supply unit. The modifications include:

  • Custom PCB Design - Multi-layer circuit board layout and component placement
  • Schematic Diagrams - Complete electrical circuit documentation
  • 3D Enclosure Design - AutoCAD drawings for the external housing
  • Component Documentation - Detailed parts lists and specifications

entry.content:
HA_LAN_RGB_Dimmer_ESP8266

An RGBW Smart Dimmer system using ESP8266 microcontroller, MQTT, and Home Assistant integration.

Overview

HA_LAN_RGB_Dimmer_ESP8266 is an IoT device built on the ESP8266 microcontroller running MicroPython. It enables remote control of RGB/RGBW LED strips via MQTT and Home Assistant. This project allows you to control color, brightness, and effects of LED lighting through MQTT messages or Home Assistant automation.

Tech Stack

  • Hardware: ESP8266 (WiFi microcontroller, e.g., NodeMCU, Wemos D1)
  • Language: Python (MicroPython on ESP8266)
  • Protocols: MQTT (remote communication), PWM (LED control), WiFi (network connectivity)
  • Integration: Home Assistant (MQTT discovery)
  • Libraries: umqttsimple (MQTT client), network utilities

Project Structure

.
├── boot.py              Initialization, configuration mode logic, WiFi connection
├── main.py              Main loop — listening for MQTT commands and updating LEDs
├── config.txt           Configuration file (WiFi, MQTT, GPIO pins)
└── index.html           Web interface for device configuration
 

How It Works

Startup & Configuration Mode

After startup, ESP8266 checks a GPIO pin. If the pin is shorted to GND, the device enters configuration mode:

  • Creates a WiFi network named ESP_RGB_Dimmer (no password)
  • Runs an HTTP server on port 80
  • Serves an HTML page (index.html) with a configuration form
  • Receives JSON configuration data and saves it to config.txt

Normal Operation Mode (Pin not shorted)

  • Loads configuration from config.txt
  • Connects to the configured WiFi network
  • Establishes connection with MQTT broker
  • main.py listens to MQTT topics for color and brightness commands
  • Updates PWM outputs to control RGB/RGBW LED strip colors and brightness
  • Supports dimming, color selection, and lighting effects

Getting Started

Step 1: Initial Configuration

  1. Upload all Python files to ESP8266
  2. Short configuration pin to GND
  3. Restart ESP8266

ESP8266 will boot in configuration mode:

  1. Connect to the ESP_RGB_Dimmer WiFi network
  2. Open your browser and navigate to http://192.168.1.1
  3. Fill out the configuration form:
    • GPIO Pins — R, G, B, W (white) channel pins
    • WiFi SSID — your network name
    • WiFi Password
    • MQTT Broker Address (e.g., mosquitto server, Home Assistant)
    • MQTT Topic — base topic for control (e.g., home/bedroom/rgb_light)
    • MQTT Username (if authentication required)
    • MQTT Password
  4. Click "Save"

Step 2: Run in Normal Mode

  1. Disconnect configuration pin from GND
  2. Restart ESP8266

The device will now boot in normal mode, connect to WiFi and MQTT. LED will blink to confirm connection.

Step 3: Control Your LEDs

Using mosquitto_pub:

# Set color to red (255, 0, 0) and brightness to 100%
mosquitto_pub -h <MQTT_SERVER> -t home/bedroom/rgb_light/set -m '{"r":255,"g":0,"b":0,"brightness":255}' -u <username> -P <password>

# Set color to blue
mosquitto_pub -h <MQTT_SERVER> -t home/bedroom/rgb_light/set -m '{"r":0,"g":0,"b":255,"brightness":255}' -u <username> -P <password>

# Dim to 50%
mosquitto_pub -h <MQTT_SERVER> -t home/bedroom/rgb_light/brightness -m '128' -u <username> -P <password>
 

Using Home Assistant:

service: mqtt.publish
data:
  topic: home/bedroom/rgb_light/set
  payload: '{"r":255,"g":0,"b":0,"brightness":255}'
 

Using Node-RED, Home Assistant, or any MQTT client:

  • Connect to your MQTT broker
  • Publish JSON messages or simple values to control:
    • Color values (RGB)
    • Brightness (0-255 PWM value)
    • On/Off commands

Features

  • 🌐 Remote LED control via MQTT from anywhere
  • 🎨 Full RGB/RGBW color control
  • 💡 Brightness dimming (0-255 PWM)
  • ⚙️ Easy web-based configuration interface
  • 🏠 Home Assistant integration via MQTT
  • 🔐 MQTT authentication support
  • 🔄 Automatic reconnection on connection loss
  • 📦 Minimal dependencies (MicroPython standard library)

Requirements

  • ESP8266 (NodeMCU, Wemos D1, or compatible)
  • MicroPython firmware
  • MQTT broker (mosquitto, Home Assistant, etc.)
  • RGB/RGBW LED strip (12V or 24V with PWM controller recommended)
  • Power supply for LED strip
  • Same local network for control

Configuration File Format

The config.txt file stores configuration in JSON format:

{
  "WiFissid": "your_wifi_name",
  "WiFipass": "your_wifi_password",
  "MQTTSrv": "mqtt.example.com",
  "MQTTBaseTopic": "home/bedroom/rgb_light",
  "MQTTUserName": "mqtt_user",
  "MQTTUserPass": "mqtt_password",
  "GPIO_R": 12,
  "GPIO_G": 13,
  "GPIO_B": 14,
  "GPIO_W": 15
}
 

MQTT Topics

Subscribe (device listens for commands):

  • {base_topic}/set — JSON with r, g, b, brightness
  • {base_topic}/color — HEX color (e.g., FF5500)
  • {base_topic}/brightness — Value 0-255
  • {base_topic}/on — Turn on (any value)
  • {base_topic}/off — Turn off

Publish (device reports state):

  • {base_topic}/state — Current color and brightness

Troubleshooting

  • Device won't connect to WiFi: Verify SSID and password are correct
  • MQTT connection fails: Check broker address, username, and password
  • LEDs not responding:
    • Verify GPIO pins are correct
    • Check MQTT topic matches configuration
    • Ensure PWM is working (test with digital multimeter)
    • Check LED strip power supply
  • Flickering or dim LEDs: Add capacitors (100µF) across power pins, use quality power supply

Hardware Wiring Example

ESP8266 Pin 12 (GPIO12) → MOSFET/PWM Controller (Red channel)
ESP8266 Pin 13 (GPIO13) → MOSFET/PWM Controller (Green channel)
ESP8266 Pin 14 (GPIO14) → MOSFET/PWM Controller (Blue channel)
ESP8266 Pin 15 (GPIO15) → MOSFET/PWM Controller (White channel)
ESP8266 GND → MOSFET GND, LED Strip GND
 

Future Enhancements

  • Support for lighting effects (fade, pulse, rainbow)
  • Multiple RGB strip groups
  • Brightness fade transitions
  • Color temperature control (Kelvin scale)
  • Hardware button controls
  • Local web dashboard for real-time control

License

This project is provided as-is for personal use.

Author

PawelZieba01

entry.content:
WiFi_Termometer-AP-WWW

A WiFi-enabled thermometer using ESP32 microcontroller with real-time temperature display and web interface.

Overview

WiFi_Termometer-AP-WWW- is an IoT device built on the ESP32 (ESP-WROOM-32) microcontroller running MicroPython. It operates as a wireless access point and web server, reading temperature from a DS18B20 sensor and displaying it on a responsive web interface. Users connect to the device's WiFi network and access the live temperature display through any web browser.

Tech Stack

  • Hardware: ESP-WROOM-32 (WiFi microcontroller), DS18B20 (1-wire temperature sensor)
  • Language: Python (MicroPython on ESP32), HTML/JavaScript
  • Protocols: WiFi (Access Point mode), HTTP (web server), 1-wire (sensor communication), DNS
  • Libraries: onewire, ds18x20 (sensor protocol), machine (GPIO control), socket (HTTP server), network (WiFi AP)

Project Structure

.
├── main.py              Main application: WiFi AP setup, HTTP server, sensor reading loop
├── microDNSSrv.py       Custom DNS server for domain resolution (MIT licensed)
├── index.html           Web UI: real-time temperature display, JavaScript polling
└── README.md            Documentation
 

How It Works

Initialization & Setup

  1. ESP32 boots and initializes as a WiFi Access Point
  2. Creates WiFi network: "Termometr WI-FI" (no password required)
  3. Assigns IP: 192.168.2.1 (subnet: 255.255.255.0)
  4. Starts DNS server that resolves any domain to device IP
  5. Starts HTTP server on port 80 listening for connections
  6. Initializes DS18B20 temperature sensor on GPIO 15
  7. Sets up LED on GPIO 2 for status indication

Normal Operation

  • Browser Connection: User connects to "Termometr WI-FI" network and navigates to:

    • http://192.168.2.1 (direct IP)
    • http://termometr.pl or any domain (resolved by DNS server)

  • Web Interface: index.html loads and starts JavaScript polling

  • Temperature Reading: JavaScript sends /getTemp request every 1 second

  • Server Response: main.py receives request, reads DS18B20 sensor, returns:

    • Current time (HH:MM:SS format)
    • Temperature value (e.g., "23.5°C")

  • Display Update: Web page updates temperature and time in real-time

  • Error Handling: If sensor is disconnected, error message blinks on page

LED Status Signals

  • Blinks every 0.4s: Waiting for WiFi device to connect
  • Blinks every 1s: Taking temperature measurement and sending data
  • Blinks rapidly (0.1s intervals): Successful WiFi connection confirmed (~2 seconds)
  • Solid on: Temperature sensor not detected
  • Off: Normal operation, waiting for browser requests

Getting Started

Requirements

  • ESP32 (ESP-WROOM-32) with MicroPython firmware installed
  • DS18B20 temperature sensor
  • LED (optional, for status indication)
  • Wiring:
    • DS18B20 data pin → GPIO 15 (configurable in main.py)
    • DS18B20 GND → GND
    • DS18B20 VCC → 3.3V (with pull-up resistor ~4.7kΩ)
    • LED anode → GPIO 2, LED cathode → GND (optional)

Step 1: Upload Files to ESP32

  1. Upload the following files to ESP32 filesystem:

    • main.py
    • microDNSSrv.py
    • index.html

  2. Ensure MicroPython is installed on your ESP32

Step 2: Power On & Connect

  1. Power on the ESP32
  2. LED will blink every 0.4s while waiting for connection
  3. Open WiFi network list on your phone/computer
  4. Connect to "Termometr WI-FI" network (no password)
  5. Open web browser and navigate to:
    • http://192.168.2.1 (recommended)
    • http://termometr.pl (or any domain)

Step 3: View Temperature

  • Temperature and time update every 1 second
  • Large display: "Temperatura: XX.X°C"
  • Time display: "HH:MM:SS"
  • If sensor is missing: Error message blinks with red text

Features

  • 🌡️ Real-time temperature monitoring via DS18B20 sensor
  • 🌐 Web-based interface accessible from any device
  • 📱 Responsive design for mobile and desktop browsers
  • 🔗 WiFi Access Point mode (no router required)
  • 📡 DNS server (any domain resolves to device)
  • 💡 Visual LED status feedback
  • 📊 JavaScript polling (updates every 1 second)
  • 🛡️ Automatic error detection and display
  • ⚙️ Minimal dependencies (MicroPython standard library)

Configuration

Adjustable Parameters in main.py

# WiFi AP Settings
ap_ip = "192.168.2.1"         # Device IP address
ap_mask = "255.255.255.0"     # Subnet mask
ap_gate = "192.168.2.1"       # Gateway
ap_ssid = "Termometr WI-FI"   # WiFi network name

# Sensor Pin
ds_pin = machine.Pin(15)      # DS18B20 data pin (change if needed)

# DNS Configuration
termo_url = "termometr.*"     # Domain pattern (e.g., termometr.pl, termometr.com, etc.)

# LED Pin
led = Pin(2, Pin.OUT)         # Status LED on GPIO 2
 

Modify RTC Time

Current code sets fixed date (2014-05-01). To use current time:

# In main.py, line 130 - replace with:
import ntptime
ntptime.settime()  # Syncs with NTP server
 

Troubleshooting

  • Device won't show up in WiFi list:

    • Verify MicroPython is properly flashed
    • Check power supply (at least 500mA recommended)

  • Browser can't connect to device:

    • Verify you're on the "Termometr WI-FI" network
    • Try both 192.168.2.1 and termometr.pl
    • Restart ESP32

  • Temperature not updating:

    • Verify DS18B20 sensor wiring (especially pull-up resistor)
    • Check GPIO 15 is not used elsewhere
    • Look for error message on page

  • Sensor always shows error:

    • Verify DS18B20 is connected to GPIO 15
    • Try higher pull-up resistor (4.7kΩ - 10kΩ)
    • Check sensor is genuine (counterfeits common)
    • Reduce cable length if using long wires

  • LED doesn't work:

    • Verify LED polarity (longer leg to GPIO 2)
    • Try different GPIO pin and update main.py
    • LED is optional and doesn't affect thermometer

Future Enhancements

  • Support for multiple DS18B20 sensors
  • Temperature logging and history graph
  • Configurable polling interval
  • MQTT integration for remote monitoring
  • Email/SMS alerts for temperature thresholds
  • Dark mode for web interface
  • WiFi password protection

License

This project is provided as-is for personal use.

Author

PawelZieba01

Paweł Zięba - 05.04.2020
